note: Gustave Behring, 28, a sergeant in the German Army, was told on his mother's deathbed that his father was George M. Pullman; she said she had been a governess in Chicago 'for a house on the west side', that Pullman promised to marry her, and, when she became pregnant, packed her off to Germany with $500. Pullman threw him out of his office; Behring was arrested again and again. Four days before Pullman's death the conversation was recorded: 'BEHRING: You are my father! PULLMAN: You are a crazy man!' 'Less than 12 hours after the funeral, Behring showed up at the family's residence on Prairie Avenue, demanding to speak to Mrs. Harriett Pullman', and was met on the steps by Pullman's sons and the family lawyers; he was arrested, found sane on 29 October 1897 and again in April 1898; detectives escorted him to the Cunard liner Campania, bound for Bremen, in September 1898; 'on June 25, 1901, Behring was again arrested at the law offices of Frank Lowden (Florence Pullman's husband) demanding $5,000 in cash and $10,000 a month for 6 months. Judge Davis, Lowden's partner, held Behring at gunpoint until the police arrived'.
